title: Phrase-briefing
goal: Two common words as one stroke (merged pairs), and the phrasing grammar (starter + auxiliary + verb as one stroke): what qualifies, how the stroke is built, which words may lose a stroke, limits.

blocks.x: A **phrase entry** is two already-settled words merged into one shorter outline: 2 strokes become 1 for a common pair. Phrase entries are ordinary dictionary entries: strike the chord, get both words. The *phrasing grammar* (one stroke built from a pronoun, auxiliary and verb keys: *I was*, *they wouldn't*, *she has been*) is the section [The phrasing grammar](#/ref/phrases/the-phrasing-grammar); [lesson 19](#/lesson/19-phrasing-grammar) and [lesson 20](#/lesson/20-phrasing-strokes) teach it.
The idea

[[of|-F]] and [[the|-T]] share no key, not even the star, so their union `-FT` is unused by anything else. That stroke is the phrase [[of the|-FT]]. *of the* is the most frequent word pair in the corpus (2,766,332,391 occurrences).
A phrase stroke is always the **bitwise union of the two words' strokes**, with no join key. Rule: **strike the keys of both words together in one stroke.**
Pressing both words' keys in one stroke differs from pressing them as two strokes, so a phrase stroke is never hit by accident while writing the two words separately.
What qualifies
A word pair (bigram) earns a phrase entry only when **all four** hold:

items: **Both words have a settled primary outline, and at least one is exactly one stroke.** "Primary" is the outline the generator chose (a brief, the plain rules reading, a spelling variant or a star-ladder step). A bonus entry (short form, alternate, backup) never counts, even when cheaper. The other word's primary may be any length.
**The one-stroke word's whole primary and the other word's first stroke share no key**, star included. When both are one stroke: the two primaries are disjoint.

**The merged outline is free, or the pair is worth more than the word that holds it** (see [Phrases compete for strokes](#/ref/phrases/phrases-compete-for-strokes)). A reserved stroke, a suffix, a hand-written `[word]` outline in `rules/briefs.toml` and another phrase are never taken.

**The pair is among the top 20,000 bigrams by raw count** (`PHRASE_TOP_N`). The count is raw, not a collocation score: pairs of two very common function words (*of the*, *in the*) are the ones worth briefing, and a collocation measure ranks them low.

blocks.x: Two eligible pairs on the same outline: the pair said more often in the corpus wins; the phrase text is the final deterministic tie-break.
Primary outlines only

A phrase is built from each word's **primary** outline, never from a bonus entry, even when the word has a cheaper one (backup, short form). A word's own primary never changes because a phrase exists; the "one single-stroke outline per word" rule is untouched.
Exception, competition for a stroke (below): a phrase may take a stroke a word holds as a *short form or alternate*, since the word keeps its primary.
A multi-stroke word in the phrase

When one word (the **filler**) has a one-stroke primary and the other (the **host**) has a primary of any length, the filler's stroke merges into the host's **first stroke only**. Later host strokes carry over unchanged, join keys included.

items: Outline = `[filler OR host's first stroke, host's remaining strokes...]`.
The merged first stroke has no join key, like any first stroke: the phrase starts a new word.
Both orders work: one-stroke word before a multi-stroke word, and multi-stroke word followed by a one-stroke word.
*added by* [[PWAEUD/+-D]]: *added* (two strokes) with *by* merged into its first stroke.

blocks.x: Other multi-stroke examples in the dictionary: `ABD/+-D` *be added*, `ADZ/+-D` *was added*, `AED/+-D` *he added*, `ABGT/+SEU` *the accuracy*, `ABT/+STRAT` *the abstract*.
About 250 phrase entries have more than one stroke; the rest are a single stroke.
The pronoun I

The word list is all lowercase, including the pronoun. The dictionary's *I* is capitalized, *I* [[EU]]; the bare letter is fingerspelled. A bigram containing *i* is looked up as *I*, and its phrase is written capitalized: *I would* is [[I would|SWROE]], not "i would". Same for *I'm*, *I'd*, *I've*, *I'll*. [[EU]] shares its vowel keys with almost every verb, so a merged *I* pair is rare; the grammar writes *I* + verb instead.
Phrases compete for strokes
A pair whose merged stroke a word already holds can take it. `in the` is `TPH` + `-T` = [[TPH-T]]; it displaced *antonio*, which moved to another outline. The pair takes the stroke when
pair count / all pairs x 25 000  >  word count / all words x (cost of its next-best outline - cost of the stolen one)

Left side: one stroke saved (a phrase has its two words' keys and one stroke fewer; a stroke weighs 25 keys, see [How short](#/ref/brevity)). Right side: what the word loses by moving. Pair counts: `bigrams_en.txt`; word counts: the subtitle frequency list.
What a phrase can never take

items: A reserved stroke, a suffix stroke, a hand-written `[word]` outline in `briefs.toml`, another phrase.
An entry settled by the star ladder, or a family-shaped entry (a family member is defined by its stem).
A **backup** (a stem plus an ending you already know): losing one costs the word nothing under the rule above, but backups are the predictable multi-stroke way in.
The **primary of a stem** (a word other words are built from). *object* keeps [[OBT]], so *on the* does not get it.

blocks.x: Protected words and the takeover limit

items: **The 5,000 most frequent words keep their primary** (`PROTECTED_WORDS`). [[on|OB]], [[want|W-T]] and [[after|AF]] stay. A phrase may still take a *short form* or *alternate* from them.

**Only the 1,000 most frequent eligible pairs may take a held stroke** (`TAKEOVER_TOP_N`). A rarer pair goes only into a free stroke. Without this limit, 373 words ended up with a star because a pair nobody will learn had taken their plain stroke.

**A word that loses its only way of being written gets another**: its next-best outline, or its best own candidate of any length that nobody holds. *antonio* moves to `TPHOEPBT`. A pair is skipped if the word would end up with nothing. A word that loses its primary is no longer part of any later phrase.
A word in a committed phrase is not taken from afterwards.

blocks.x: Size of the result

Current build: 7,213 merged and borrowed phrase entries (`02-lyk-phrases.json`) and 3,758 grammar phrases (`02-lyk-phrasing.json`). 87 merged phrases took a stroke from a rarer word. A merge joins two strokes you know into one: *in the* is the stroke for *in* plus the stroke for *the*.
Phrases borrowed from other dictionaries

Plover, Lapwing and the fifteen other theories ([other theories' briefs](#/ref/collisions)) also write two-word phrases as one stroke: `O*T` *to the*, `TKW-PBLT` *do not*. Some pairs cannot merge (shared key) or merge onto a stroke a word holds. For those the pass offers the dictionaries' one-stroke phrases, in the same arbitration as a merge, ranked by pair frequency. Rules:

items: **The merge comes first.** If the pair merges and the stroke is free (or a word gives it up), the pair is the merge. A borrowed outline is a fallback, tried cheapest first; a pair is committed once.
**A borrowed phrase never competes with a merge for a stroke.** If any pair's own merge produces that stroke, the borrowed outline is dropped.
**Same takeover limits.** A borrowed pair takes a stroke from a word only among the 1,000 commonest candidates, never from a top-5,000 word's primary, and only when worth more than the word loses.
**Only one-stroke, typable outlines of two plain lowercase words.** A phrase with a number or a capital is skipped, as is anything on a key lyk does not have.

blocks.x: [[to the|TOTD]], [[on the|O*LT]] and [[to be|TORB]] have one-stroke phrases. A borrowed phrase must be memorized; a merge can be worked out, hence the merge first.
Not covered

items: **Both words multi-stroke.** At least one side must be a one-stroke filler.
**Three or more words in a merged pair.** No chaining of merged phrases (unlike backups, which chain: *green* + *house* = *greenhouse*, then + `+-Z`). The grammar writes two to five words.
**A backup or short form as a component.** Only primaries are used.
**Removing a join-key boundary inside an existing multi-stroke word.** A different mechanism.

blocks.x: The phrasing grammar

One stroke writes a **starter** (who), an **auxiliary** (when, which modal, not) and a **verb**, each on its own region of the board, so no combination overlaps another: [[I was|SWREB]], [[they wouldn't|STWHRO*E]], [[she has been|SKWH-FB]]. 8 starters, 5 modals, 3 special verbs and 20 verbs (about 36 parts) give **3,758 phrases**, all written to `02-lyk-phrasing.json` by `src/phrases/grammar.rs` from the tables in `rules/grammar.toml`. Typing it is taught in [lesson 19](#/lesson/19-phrasing-grammar) and [lesson 20](#/lesson/20-phrasing-strokes).

blocks.x: The verb codes
The codes are worked out by a rule, not listed (`Grammar::derive_codes`); the verbs are taken in the order of `rules/grammar.toml`, commonest first, after *be*, *have* and *have been*:

items: The code is the verb's **final consonants** written on the right bank by the rules (`rules/plover.toml`): *get* [[-T]], *come* [[-PL]], *want* [[-PBT]], *find* [[-PBD]], *think* [[-PBG]] (a star a coda cluster carries is left off: the star is *not*).
A verb that ends in a vowel uses its **first** consonant: *say* [[-S]], *go* [[-G]], *know* [[-PB]].

If a commoner verb has that code, add the verb's **first consonant**: *take* [[-BGT]] (*make* has [[-BG]]), *feel* [[-FL]] (*tell* has [[-L]]), *give* [[-FG]] (*have* has [[-F]]), *mean* [[-PBL]], *seem* [[-PLS]], *look* [[-BLG]].
If that is taken too, add **[[-Z]]**: *see* [[-SZ]], *like* [[-BLGZ]].

blocks.x: Where the grammar is placed

items: **Before any word settles**, like the standalone suffixes: after the reserved strokes, the suffixes, the pronoun *I* and every hand-written `[word]` outline in `rules/briefs.toml`, and before the words' own candidates compete. The words never see a starter stroke as free.

**A held stroke is never taken.** A stroke already held by a reserved entry, a suffix or a hand-written brief leaves its phrase out (none does: all 3,758 are placed); `lyk build --report` lists any phrase left out and what holds its stroke. A word whose own candidates land on a grammar stroke has not got it yet, so it settles on its next outline.

**The words that moved.** 122 words changed an outline that is not a backup; of the 5,000 commonest only [[pity|P*EUTD]] (was `KPWR`) and [[impress|EUPL/+PRES]] (was `KPWRES`) changed their primary. Every word keeps an outline; the weighted keys per stroke is unchanged (3.252).

**Merged pairs leave these texts to the grammar.** A pair the grammar writes (*it is*, *I was*, *he could*) gets no merged stroke; 149 merged phrases that wrote one of its texts were dropped, so *it is* is [[it is|KPWH-B]], not `ST`.
A grammar phrase is never taken by a merged pair or a borrowed phrase, and is not a stem the stroke read-back continues.

blocks.x: Looking a phrase up

items: `lyk lookup "they wouldn't"` (and the interactive lookup) puts the grammar's stroke first, marked as a phrase, with the key group that says each part (`STWHR starter (they) + OE auxiliary (would) + * not`), then each word as usual. Case, punctuation, a curly apostrophe, *I'm* / *they're* / *I've* / *I'll* and a spelt-out negative (*do not*, *can not*, *cannot*) are read as the grammar's own text.
A text the grammar covers only at its start (*she has been going*) names the part it covers (*she has been*, 3 of 4 words) and answers the rest word by word.
`lyk lookup SWRAB` explains a grammar stroke part by part: *I can be*, `SWR` starter, `A` auxiliary, `-B` verb.

The lessons site's Lookup does the same from `data/grammar.json`. The keymux live lookup (`keymux steno lookup`) does not: it answers a phrase word by word and does not match a whole phrase entry by its text, so look the stroke up there (it types the phrase, `SWRAB` is *I can be*).

items: Questions (*do you*, *are you*, *can I*): the starter after the auxiliary.
*that*, *this*, *what*, *who* as starters; contracted positives (*I'm*, *it's*); other verbs.

blocks.x: Where it runs

Merged and borrowed phrases are one pass, run once after the backup pass settles and before the "stranded" diagnostic is computed; it sees the final dictionary, backups included. The grammar is placed earlier, before any word settles (see [The phrasing grammar](#/ref/phrases/the-phrasing-grammar)), and the merged pass skips every text the grammar writes. Phrase entries have their own origins (`Phrase`, `Grammar`); the stroke read-back never treats a phrase as a word: a continuation stroke after `-FT` is not read as *of the* plus an ending. See [the stroke read-back](#/ref/fallback).
What it saves

The quote benchmark walks a passage left to right, taking the longest phrase entry (merged pair or grammar phrase, up to five words) that covers the next words. Phrases save **strokes**, not keys: a merged phrase's key count is exactly the sum of its two words' key counts; the stroke count drops by one per hit (a grammar phrase spends more keys than the words' primaries and saves the strokes of every word it covers but one).

Quote benchmark, merged phrases and grammar together: the phrase-aware walk uses 974 strokes on the 103 hand-picked passages (1,225 word by word) and 4,886 on the 416 extracted ones (5,915): about 20% and 17% fewer. On running prose (five novels, 712,328 words) the grammar saves 1.6% of strokes over the merged phrases alone; passages of speech and messages have more *I*, *you* and *it* pairs per word.
A bigram limit of 40,000 would save about 1.6% more strokes but add around 13,500 phrases to learn; rejected.
